claims.text: The unified mechanical behavior of HfNbTaTiZr is governed by thermally induced internal residual stresses.
The internal residual stresses originate from intrinsic thermal-expansion mismatch among Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr.
Composite solidification and thermal cycling enhance the mismatch-driven residual stresses.
Mismatch-driven stresses modify local lattice distortions and dislocation dynamics.
Conventionally processed cast or cold-rolled HfNbTaTiZr is expected to contain some elemental segregation and residual stress.
Slow cooling or composite solidification will enhance thermal-expansion-mismatch effects by promoting differential thermal contraction.
Rapid homogenization and quenching will minimize mismatch-induced residual-stress development.
Differential thermal contraction between constituent elements creates a network of internal residual stresses and local lattice distortions.
The disparate thermal-expansion coefficients of Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr cause nonuniform contraction during cooling.
At lower temperatures, residual stresses increase elastic stiffness and elastic moduli through lattice hardening.
At high temperatures, mismatch-induced stress fields pin dislocations and reduce tensile-creep rates.
During cold rolling and aging at 600–800 °C, residual stresses promote work hardening and recovery processes that enhance microhardness and strength.
Relative to the baseline, mismatch-enhanced samples will have higher microhardness after cold rolling.
Relative to the baseline, mismatch-enhanced samples will have higher elastic moduli over 293–1100 K.
Relative to the baseline, mismatch-enhanced samples will have lower tensile-creep rates at 1250 °C.
Relative to the baseline, mismatch-enhanced samples will exhibit greater hardening after aging at 600–800 °C because residual stress stabilizes local order.
Approximately 1 wt.% oxygen may independently alter the measured mechanical and thermoelastic properties.
